Legislative Accomplishments
Solving local constituent issues and working on legislation are the primary duties of a senator.  Below is a list of some of the laws Senator Argall has successfully authored:
SB 157
In 2018, the Public Assistance Integrity Act was signed into law. This law closed a loophole that did not require lottery winnings to be considered as income when determining eligibility for benefits.
To ensure compliance with this Act, Senate Bill 157 was introduced to require the Department of Human Services to submit an annual report on details of how lottery winnings and the average equity value of vehicles were counted for cash assistance. This was done to ensure that lottery winners are not receiving cash benefits if they reached the monetary thresholds as established in the 2018 law.
This report requires details on the number of annual applicants reporting lottery winnings of $600 or more, the number of applicants that were denied benefits due to their lottery winnings, details on potential gaps in communication between the department and county assistance offices which may have resulted in failed reporting of winnings, and details regarding ongoing strategies between the department and the State Lottery to accurately report lottery winning and determination of benefits.
This legislation was incorporated into the Human Services Code of 2025.
Act 46 of 2025
SB 156
This legislation was introduced to require the Department of Human Services to check wage records by employers and the Department of Revenue against recipients of Medical Assistance and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits to fight back against waste, fraud, and abuse within these programs. From 2019 to 2023, the Pennsylvania Office of State Inspector General filed more than 2,900 criminal complaints of welfare fraud, and more than $15 million owed in restitution.
This bill was incorporated into the Human Services Code of 2025
Act 46 of 2025
SB 155
This legislation was introduced to crack down on the abuse of our Human Services programs and ensure that SNAP benefits aren’t being spent on those who are no longer living by requiring the Department of Human Services to check death certificates with the Department of Health’s Bureau of Vital Statistics against its recipients of Medical Assistance and SNAP benefits. A state audit previously found 2,324 deceased public assistance recipients received benefits totaling $700,000 in a 12-month period.
This bill was incorporated into Human Services Code of 2025

This legislation was initially introduced following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. According to the 2020 census, Schuylkill County has the highest percentage of people with Ukrainian ancestry in the United States.
Companies are now banned from receiving Pennsylvania state contracts, grants, or tax credits if they are owned or affiliated with the governments of Russia or Belarus.

This law established the Office of Deputy Attorney General for Organized Retail Crime Theft to pursue the leaders of these criminal rings and also lowered the thresholds for the value of good to constitute third degree and second degree felonies while also creating the threshold for a new first degree felony.
Act No. 42 of 2023
Senator Argall led a coalition of Senators to voice support for funding the Office of Deputy Attorney General for Organized Retail Crime Theft as part of the 2024-2025 Budget. As a result, $2.72 million was added to the new office to carry out its operations of pursuing leaders of criminal rings engaged in organized retail crime theft.
Act No. 1A of 2024
SB 748
In 2018, Senator Argall was the sponsor of Act 86 to reduce the number of accidents and fatalities of highway construction workers and motorists by allowing the use of speed cameras in active work zones. In just five years, speeding in work zones dropped 20% while crashes dropped 19% and fatalities dropped 6%.
Speed cameras were also placed along Roosevelt Boulevard in Philadelphia, one of the most dangerous roads in the country.
SB 748 was introduced to make the program permanent (under Act 86, the program was offered for only five years). The premise of this bill was amended into a House bill which was also focused on road safety and was signed into law by the Governor on December 14, 2023.

This legislation brought Pennsylvania into the Interstate Teacher Mobility Compact to help certified teachers relocating to Pennsylvania to continue teaching.
teachers who hold a compact-eligible certification can apply for the closest equivalent certification without having to complete additional materials, exams or coursework.
This bill also incorporated key provisions of the 2023 Education Code.

Since 1970, 90 PennDOT workers have died while carrying out their duties. Senate Bill 900 was drafted to name ten local bridges in their memory.
This bill was amended into similar legislation which was signed into law by the Governor on October 21, 2023.

SB 106
This constitutional amendment was introduced to allow gubernatorial candidates to select their own running mate in a manner similar to the process in which Presidential candidates select their running mates. This was done in order to provide greater trust in the executive branch to delegate duties while avoiding potential division and friction between the two office holders which has happened in the past.
The House and Senate later amended the bill to provide for additional ballot questions including a provision to limit executive orders/proclamations to 21 days unless further extended by the legislature, a provision which states that the legislature’s disapproval of a regulation would be required to be sent to the Governor, a provision that would require voters to present some sort of ID prior to voting, a provision clarifying that the State Constitution does not grant the right to a taxpayer-funded abortion, and a provision requiring the legislature to provide for the auditing of elections.
Because this bill is a constitutional amendment, SB 106 must pass both the Senate and the House of Representatives again during the 2023-2024 Session before it is presented to the voters for a final decision.

Senator David G. Argall represents the 29th District, which now includes 102 municipalities in the anthracite region including all of Schuylkill and Carbon Counties, and parts of Luzerne County including the city of Hazleton.
The proud grandson of Cornish, Welsh, and German farmers, coal miners, and factory workers, Senator Argall’s top legislative priority is revitalizing our downtowns and older industrial neighborhoods.
Senator Argall has led successful battles to pass several new anti-blight laws.  Because of his grassroots teamwork, “left behind” communities across Pennsylvania, from his hometown of Tamaqua to parts of our largest cities, have witnessed a positive transformation.
In the Senate, he chaired a bipartisan commission which unanimously recommended more than $400 million in taxpayer savings.  Senator Argall is also a leader in conservation, farmland preservation, and abandoned mine reclamation initiatives, locally as a volunteer Scout leader and as the author of legislation which has recycled more than 97 percent of Pennsylvania’s waste tires.  The National Eagle Scout Association, due to his “distinguished service to his profession and community,” presented him with the Outstanding Eagle Scout Award.
Senator Argall earned a bachelor’s degree from Lycoming College and a Ph.D. in public administration from Penn State.  His studies included an Eisenhower Fellowship to review the economic and political transformations in Germany after the fall of the Berlin Wall.  His doctoral dissertation reviewed the benefits and drawbacks of Pennsylvania’s tax-free “Keystone Opportunity Zones” for economic development.
Dr. Argall has served as a part-time public policy instructor at Lycoming College, Penn State, and at Lehigh Carbon Community College, where he led the transformation of a vacant junior high school where his parents once taught into LCCC’s Morgan Center.
Senator Argall and his wife Beth are the parents of AJ and Elise, who are pursuing careers in patent law and communications. The Argalls share their Rush Township home with two very active terriers, Maggie and Wolfgang.

Veterans and their spouses are being targeted by a new postcard scam advertising a fraudulent “Veterans Saving Program.” The mailer claims eligibility for an extra $185 monthly payment and dental benefits, but the program does not exist.

Under a new law,

I also highlighted the bipartisan actions of the Statewide Blight Task Force which I chair, including Act 90 of 2010, which gave local municipalities more tools for code enforcement, Act 153 of 2012, which created the modern-day land bank, and Act 152 of 2016, which grants counties funding for demolition. Thanks to Act 152, 32 of Pennsylvania’s 67 counties have completed over $31 million in successful county demolition efforts.
While this progress is important, we still have MUCH work to do!

Higher education is getting closer to home—and that’s a big win for our region!

I find it deeply troubling that
Governor Shapiro has joined a lawsuit

Welcoming Temple Dental Students to Tamaqua
Rep. Jamie Barton and I recently joined the Tamaqua Area Chamber of Commerce to welcome students at the Temple Dental Education Center and Clinic in downtown Tamaqua.
Eighteen local businesses and organizations partnered to provide the new students with gifts to encourage the dental students to explore Tamaqua and the surrounding region. Read more here.
In another effort to address rural health care, Tamaqua native and Misericordia University student Alexis Bowman is collecting donations for a “dental goodie bag” drive she is organizing. She’s collecting basic dental necessities including toothbrushes, dental floss, toothpaste and mouthwash, and plans to distribute them to Volunteers in Medicine Wilkes-Barre, Mom-n-PA, Women in Crisis (Pottsville), Child Development, the Salvation Army and any others who need dental supplies. Developed by Matthew Pezon, the project represents more than $2.1 million in private investment, transforming an entire block of blighted and decaying properties into 12 revitalized single-family homes and eight apartments.
With new jobs continuing to come to our region, the demand for affordable, quality housing continues to grow. Investments like this are helping create much-needed new housing opportunities and breathe new life into Pottsville and our region.

This project will help design a new mine drainage treatment for the abandoned Pine Forest Shaft and help clean the Upper Schuylkill River.
While existing mining companies are responsible to reclaim their properties, many other abandoned sites remain across PA. Penn State’s Local Campuses Are Too Important to Lose
This recent Pittsburgh Post-Gazette story
about Penn State closing some of its small local campuses is an important reminder of just how much was at stake for our region last year.
A year and a half ago, our communities came together—students, faculty, employers, educators, legislators and other local leaders, and thousands of residents, including Republicans, Democrats and Independents, through emails and petitions to the University’s Board of Trustees —to make the case that Penn State Hazleton and Penn State Schuylkill are far too important to us to lose, with growing enrollments, beautiful, modern campuses, with the potential to grow even larger in the future.
The evidence we all demonstrated at multiple public hearings here was compelling. Today, because of that comprehensive effort, both campuses remain open, giving students across our region access to an affordable Penn State education close to home and providing local employers with a vital workforce pipeline.
Our work isn’t finished. We need to continue supporting these campuses, growing enrollment, and expanding programs, so that both campuses remain strong for generations to come—for ALL of us!
Strengthening Pennsylvania’s CDL Laws
After the terrible accident which cost State Trooper Michael Pahira his life on I-81 near Minersville in July, especially considering the horrifying details outlined in this article, many local people have been asking me to strengthen our laws regarding unqualified truck drivers.
I find it deeply troubling that Governor Shapiro has joined a lawsuit challenging federal access to state commercial driver’s license (CDL) records. For nearly four decades, CDL information systems have helped states and federal transportation officials identify disqualified or unqualified commercial drivers and keep dangerous operators off our roads.
The General Assembly recently acted with Act 50 of 2026, which I supported. The measure cracks down on unauthorized CDL mills. The Senate also passed Senate Bill 1295 and Senate Bill 1296 to strengthen commercial driver qualifications, English proficiency requirements, and disqualification standards. Both bills are awaiting action in the PA House.
The loss of Trooper Pahira is a painful reminder that we must do everything we can to make sure every commercial driver on our highways is properly trained, properly licensed, and qualified to operate a tractor-trailer safely.

Fighting Crime: Hazleton Hearing Examines Trends & Prevention
As Chairman of the Senate Majority Policy Committee, I recently joined Rep. Dane Watro and Rep. David Rowe to chair a public hearing focused on crime trends, public safety and the challenges facing law enforcement across Pennsylvania.
We heard directly from Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday, local District Attorneys Sam Sanguedolce and Mike O’Pake, local police chiefs, Luzerne County Sheriff Genesis Arias, and community organizations.
There was encouraging news: crime is declining in many areas, fentanyl cases and overdose deaths are down, property crime in our region, and specifically Hazleton, has decreased, and school violence has dropped significantly. We also heard that the Organized Retail Theft Unit, which was created by a law I wrote, has topped more than 100 investigations in its first full year. But there is still a lot of work to do.
We discussed the need to support law enforcement, address blight and other root causes of crime, combat fentanyl and human trafficking, protect victims, and ensure our criminal justice system holds dangerous offenders accountable. We also discussed the urgent need for the PA House to immediately pass
Senate Bill 1400
, which sets sentencing guidelines for felony murder after the PA Supreme Court ruled that mandatory life sentences for this crime are unconstitutional.
You can learn more about this issue here.
I look forward to continuing to work together to make Hazleton and communities across Pennsylvania safer places to live, work and raise a family.
Read more about the hearing here.
Why are Electricity Prices Rising, and What Can PA Do About It?
I recently chaired a Senate Majority Policy Committee hearing in Shenandoah to examine a problem that is hitting families and businesses across Pennsylvania: rising electric bills.
The solution starts with a simple principle — we need more energy production, not more restrictions on producing energy.
Pennsylvania has tremendous energy resources, including natural gas, coal, and coal refuse. At the same time, electricity demand is growing. If we continue retiring reliable power plants faster than we build new generation, consumers will continue to face higher costs and greater reliability concerns. That is especially true when neighboring states continue to shut down reliable generation and rely on the same regional PJM electric grid.
We also heard about the important role Schuylkill County’s coal refuse power plants play. These facilities generate electricity while cleaning up mine-scarred land, restoring streams and creating good-paying jobs.
We can meet our growing energy needs and protect our environment. Pennsylvania has made tremendous progress in cleaning up the environmental damage of the past, and we should continue that progress while making sure families can afford to heat and power their homes.
The goal should be clear: more reliable Pennsylvania energy, fewer unnecessary regulations, and more affordable electric bills.
Measure Cracking Down on “CDL Mills” Becomes Law
After the terrible accident which cost State Trooper Mike Pahira his life on I-81 near Minersville in July, many local people have been asking me to strengthen our laws regarding unqualified truck drivers.
Legislation to eliminate unauthorized commercial driver’s license (CDL) schools in Pennsylvania is now law, significantly boosting penalties for these “CDL mills.”
Act 50 of 2026
increases the maximum civil penalty for operating an unauthorized CDL school from $2,500 to $25,000, giving the state Department of Education a stronger enforcement tool to stop illegal operations and discourage violations.
The Senate also passed
Senate Bill 1295
and
Senate Bill 1296
to reinforce tractor trailer safety in the commonwealth. The legislative package reflects new federal regulations and federal legislation to strengthen commercial vehicle operations following allegations of unqualified truck drivers in the country illegally.
Read more about improving commercial vehicle safety here
.
My Bill to Remove Employment Barriers for Cosmetologists Signed into Law
My legislation to streamline licensing for the cosmetology workforce has been signed into law by the Governor, a major step in addressing Pennsylvania’s ongoing workforce shortages.
With salons and small businesses across Pennsylvania struggling to find enough licensed professionals, this new law will make it far easier for experienced cosmetologists to continue their careers.  There is no reason why a cosmetologist in good standing should need to start from scratch just because they crossed a state border. This bipartisan law cuts through bureaucracy and supports employers who are desperate for qualified workers

My office hosts monthly Veteran Service Officer Days to help veterans and their loved ones navigate and apply for benefits earned through military service.
Our next scheduled date is Tuesday, September 22, in my Mahanoy City Office. For an appointment, please call (570) 773-0891.
State Budget Supports Veterans and Their Families
On July 12, we finalized the 2026-27 state budget that included creating and enhancing programs and services aimed at assisting Pennsylvania veterans and their families such as:
Providing a 6.3% increase for tuition assistance to children of honorably discharged veterans who have service-connected disabilities and served during a period of war or armed conflict and children of veterans who die or died in service during a period of war or armed conflict.
Providing a 10.2% increase for the

, which gives eligible veterans a $150 monthly pension.

New Law Connects Families of Deceased Services Members with Support
To better connect families with their local veterans’ affairs office, the General Assembly unanimously passed
Senate Bill 130
, now Act 42 of 2026, which requires funeral directors and cemeteries to provide the family of a deceased serviceperson contact information for the county director of veterans’ affairs. They must also notify the county director of veterans’ affairs of the death of a service person within 96 hours of receiving their remains.
Pennsylvania county veteran’s affairs offices are available to better assist veterans with access to benefits for which they might be eligible, and

Honoring Veterans with Visual Impairments with a Capitol Monument
A Braille Flag monument honoring veterans with visual impairments could be installed at the Pennsylvania Capitol Building under legislation passed by the Senate and sent to the House of Representatives for consideration.
The Braille Flag was created to honor the service of veterans who have been left with life-long visual disabilities. Under
Senate Bill 1303
, the monument would be made of bronze and include the Pledge of Allegiance in Braille.
The display would be sponsored by the Moose Lodge and the American Braille Flag Project, a non-profit organization dedicated to the placement of these flags throughout the country.
Read more about Senate Bill 1303 here

The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs’
Homeless Aging and Disabled Veterans Initiative
aims to help homeless veterans with chronic, complex health needs secure affordable housing within their communities or transition more easily to any higher levels of care they need. The initiative works to better integrate home and community healthcare, social services and permanent supportive housing.

PENNSYLVANIA SENATE REPUBLICAN CAUCUS PRIVACY POLICY
PENNSYLVANIA SENATE REPUBLICAN CAUCUS PRIVACY POLICY
Effective Date: March 18, 2025
The Pennsylvania Senate Republican Caucus (“we,” “our,” or “us”) is committed to safeguarding your privacy. This Privacy Policy explains how we collect, use, share, and protect your information. By using our website or engaging with our communications, you agree to the terms of this Privacy Policy.
Personally identifiable information may be disclosed in response to legal process, for example, in response to a court order or a subpoena. We also may disclose such information in response to a law enforcement agency’s request, or where we believe it is necessary to investigate, prevent, or take action regarding illegal activities, suspected fraud, situations involving potential threats to the physical safety of any person, violations of our terms of use, to verify or enforce compliance with the policies governing our website and applicable laws or as otherwise required or permitted by law or consistent with legal requirements. Employees and legislators of the Pennsylvania Senate Republican Caucus who have access to personally identifiable information (PII) are required to protect this information in a manner that is consistent with this Privacy Policy by, for example, not using the information for any purpose other than to carry out the services they are performing.
Although appropriate measures to safeguard against unauthorized disclosures of information is taken, it cannot be fully guaranteed that PII that we collect will never be disclosed in a manner that is inconsistent with this Privacy Policy.
INFORMATION WE COLLECT
Automatically Collected Data
We automatically collect non-personally identifiable information when you visit our website, such as:
IP address (anonymized to ensure privacy)
Browser type and version
Device type (e.g., desktop, mobile)
Geographic location (general, not specific)
Pages visited, time spent on pages, and navigation paths
Referral sources (e.g., links from other websites)
Information You Provide
We may collect personal information directly from you, such as:
Name, address, and contact details (e.g., email address, phone number)
Survey responses
Newsletter subscription information
Use of Information
We use the information we collect to:
Monitor and improve website performance;
Enhance user experience and accessibility;
Communicate with you regarding events, services, and legislative updates; and/or
Comply with legal obligations.
GOOGLE ANALYTICS
The Pennsylvania Senate Republican Caucus values your privacy. This section explains how we use Google Analytics on our website to understand visitor behavior and improve the user experience while safeguarding your data.
Information Collected via Google Analytics
We do not collect or process PII through Google Analytics. Google Analytics uses cookies and similar technologies to collect the following types of non-personally identifiable information:
IP address (anonymized to ensure privacy)
Browser type and version
Device type (e.g., desktop, mobile)
Geographic location (general, not specific)
Pages visited, time spent on pages, and navigation paths
Referral sources (e.g., links from other websites)
Purpose of Data Collection
We use the aggregated data from Google Analytics to:
Monitor and analyze website performance;
Improve website content, navigation, and accessibility;
Identify and address technical issues; and/or
Optimize public service delivery.
Cookies
Google Analytics uses cookies to collect data about website usage. You can manage or disable cookies in your browser settings. Disabling cookies may impact your user experience but will not prevent access to the site. For more information about how Google uses cookies, visit Google’s Privacy Policy:
https://policies.google.com/privacy
.
Data Sharing and Security
Third-Party Access: We do not share Google Analytics data with third parties unless required by law or for authorized security purposes.
Data Security: All data is stored securely and anonymized to protect user privacy.
Opt-Out Options
You can opt out of Google Analytics tracking by:
Installing the Google Analytics Opt-out Browser Add-on; and/or
Adjusting your browser settings to block cookies.
SMS TEXTING
We understand that the privacy of your information is important to you. This privacy policy describes how we collect, use, and share information from individuals that consent to receive texts messages from us.
Information We Collect
Personal information: When you consent to receive text messages from the Senate of Pennsylvania, we may collect your first name, last name, address, email address, caller id, and phone number.
How This Information is Used
We use this information for the following purposes:
To respond to your inquiries by email, text, or phone;
To complete and fulfill any requests for services or support;
In accordance with any consent you have provided;
As legally necessary, to include complying with a subpoena, court order or legal process;
To correspond with you in furtherance of official Commonwealth business; and/or
To conduct official Commonwealth business and governmental functions as permitted by law.
We do not collect or use Personal Information for commercial marketing. We will not disclose, sell, or rent Personal Information collected, except as otherwise provided for by law.
How This Information is Shared
We retain and use the information you provide for internal use only and will not sell, transfer, disclose, or distribute your personal information or SMS consent to any third party unless needed by the consented-to service. Except to the extent that you are participating in a live program, we will retain and utilize the information you provide for internal use only and will not sell, transfer, disclose, or distribute your personal information to any third party.
SMS Consent and Mobile Messaging Terms & Conditions
We operate a mobile messaging program (the “Program”) subject to these SMS Consent and Mobile Messaging Terms and Conditions (these “Mobile Messaging Terms”). The Program and our collection and use of your personal information are also subject to this Privacy Policy. By enrolling, signing up, or otherwise agreeing to participate in the Program, you accept and agree to these Mobile Messaging Terms and this Privacy Policy.
1. Program Description: If you have consented to receive text messages from us, you may receive texts about customer service, legislative support inquires, or conversational texts. Message frequency will vary. You agree that we, our affiliates, and any third-party service providers may send you messages regarding the foregoing topics. We do not charge for mobile messages sent through the Program, but you are responsible for any message and data rates imposed by your mobile provider, as standard data and message rates may apply for short message service and multimedia messages.
1.1 Types of text messages – Information on legislation or legislative events, office hours inquiry, help to fill out a government form or government process, and to respond to inquiries initiated by you.
2. User Opt-In: By providing your mobile phone number to us, you are voluntarily opting in to the Program and you agree to receive recurring mobile messages from us at the mobile phone number associated with your opt-in, even if such number is registered on any state or federal “Do Not Call” list. You agree that any mobile phone number you provide to us is a valid mobile phone number of which you are the owner or authorized user. Your participation in the Program is completely voluntary.
3. User Opt-Out and Support: You may opt-out of the Program at any time. If you wish to opt-out of the Program and stop receiving mobile messages from us, or you no longer agree to these Mobile Messaging Terms, reply STOP to the mobile number the message is sent from. You understand and agree that the foregoing is the only reasonable method of opting out. If you want to join the Program again, just sign up as you did the first time, and we will start sending messages to you again. For support, reply HELP to the mobile number the message is sent from or review this Privacy Policy. Our mobile messaging platform may not recognize requests that modify the foregoing commands, and you agree that we and our service providers will not be liable for failing to honor requests that do not comply with the requirements in these Mobile Messaging Terms.
4. Disclaimer of Warranty and Liability: The Program is offered on an “as-is” basis and may not be available in all areas, at all times, or on all mobile providers. You agree that neither we nor our service providers will be liable for any failed, delayed, or misdirected delivery of any mobile message or information sent through the Program.
5. Modifications: We may modify or cancel the Program or any of its features at any time, with or without notice. To the extent permitted by applicable law, we may also modify these Mobile Messaging Terms at any time. Any such modification will take effect when it is posted to our website. You agree to review these Mobile Messaging Terms periodically to ensure that you are aware of any modifications. Your continued participation in the Program will constitute your acceptance of those modifications.
COMPLIANCE WITH LAWS
We comply with all laws applicable to the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.
UPDATES AND CONTACT INFORMATION
This Privacy Policy may be updated periodically. Please review this page for changes. If you have any questions about this Privacy Policy or our privacy practices, please contact us at 717-787-6725.

Reducing the Negative Impacts of Social Media on Students
On Thursday, I chaired a public hearing of the Senate Majority Policy Committee focused on the negative impacts of social media on our students.
We heard from Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday, students, parents, mental health advocates, and others about the serious challenges young people face online, from harmful content and AI-generated abuse to the effects of excessive social media use on mental health and learning.
Attorney General Sunday shared an update on his office’s efforts to protect children online and hold technology companies accountable. His office recently reached a significant agreement with Facebook parent company Meta, which secured over $516 million for youth mental health support and sets time restrictions, age verification requirements, and limits on inappropriate content for minors. Sunday has filed similar lawsuits against TikTok and Snapchat.
Hearing directly from those affected, and those working to protect our kids, is invaluable as we work toward realistic solutions to protect our children.
Progress in Breathing New Life into Downtown Pottsville
Big things are happening in Pottsville, breathing much-needed new life into vacant downtown buildings! The PA Downtown Center recently brought more than 70 economic development managers to Pottsville for its Leadership Forum with Mayor Tom Smith, City Council, and the Pottsville Area Development Corporation.
They reviewed several new businesses and toured the ongoing expansion of the Miners 1928 Hotel, which will add 66 additional rooms.  Until recently, it was a beautiful but very large vacant bank and an empty hotel.
One announcement really stole the show! The new hotel’s owner Bill Metzinger unveiled plans for the former Pomeroy’s Department Store’s transformation into a Yuengling-themed sports bar just down the street from America’s oldest brewery.
Yuengling already attracts nearly 70,000 visitors to our region each year and this project has the potential to greatly increase the number of people visiting Pottsville. As Bill told the
Republican Herald
, he hopes the project will be “the dynamite that explodes downtown development.”
Read more here.
One Step Closer for a New Use of the White Haven Center
Our goal to breathe new life into the long-vacant White Haven Center moved one step further this week.
The PA Senate and the House of Representatives have approved the 2026 Real Property Disposition Plan, which authorizes the sale of the White Haven Center through competitive bidding or public auction. This 182-acre and 23 building campus has sat vacant since 2023, while the state’s bureaucracy continues to spend millions of dollars each year maintaining it. The next step is to move toward a sale and, ultimately, put this property back into productive use.
Rep. Jamie Walsh and I have heard directly from residents and local leaders about the importance of finding a new purpose for this property. Luzerne County is also completing a study to evaluate the best potential redevelopment options for the property—and the sooner, the better!
Progress at the Schwab School in Weatherly
Finally!! Efforts to transform the historic Mrs. C.M. Schwab School in Weatherly are moving forward. After three decades of blight and decay, this 1901 landmark is on track to be transformed into 30 affordable apartments, while preserving the character and history of this important building.
Rep. Doyle Heffley and I have worked with the Alliance for Building Communities and Weatherly’s borough council to secure more than $2.2 million in competitive state funding and housing tax credits for the project. Most recently, Weatherly received $459,838 in state Local Share Account funding to demolish the deteriorating Schwab School annex, an important step in moving the project forward.
Local journalist Ruth Isenberg put it best: “The building, well-constructed though it is, it has begun to show signs of deterioration. What was once a beautiful and generous gift to the community was beginning to turn into a dangerous eyesore. The community needs housing. The Schwab school is a piece of history that should be used, not abandoned. It has sat idle and unoccupied for too long. Restoring Damaged Mine Lands Throughout Carbon, Luzerne, and Schuylkill Counties
This week, I was invited to serve as the keynote speaker at the Eastern PA Coalition for Abandoned Mine Reclamation’s Annual Conference near Harrisburg. I shared how much progress we’ve made since my friends and I from Tamaqua’s East End used to explore the abandoned coal mines literally across the road from our homes.
Landscapes that were once black and gray are now lush and green—or, this time of year, brilliant shades of red and yellow. Streams that once ran orange and black are now clear, with fish swimming through them. And massive holes in the landscape have been filled in and reclaimed.
As an original sponsor of Pennsylvania’s Growing Greener program, I understand how important these public-private partnerships are to make our communities healthier, more attractive places to live and create new opportunities for future generations. But we also know there is MUCH more work to be done!
Good News at Penn State Schuylkill & Penn State Hazleton!
The Penn State Schuylkill Advisory Board recently shared some VERY positive news:
The Fall 2026 student body includes 222 NEW students from 13 different states.
The number of students living on campus has increased nearly 25% since last year.
Several infrastructure projects are moving forward across the campus.
Several new faculty members have arrived on campus.
Eight local high schools will visit the campus by the end of November.
The campus is experiencing record participation in collegiate sports, with 267 athletes this year, a 27% increase from last year.
The Campus’ award-winning Cooperative Education Program has added 34 new students, as well as multiple new businesses and organizations to the consortium of employers.
At Penn State Hazleton, Dr. Menah Pratt has hit the ground running in her new role as Northeast Regional Chancellor. She recently shared her plans to expand outreach to the Greater Hazleton community, strengthen partnerships with local colleges and businesses, recruit students for the 2027-28 academic year, and establish a new regional leadership academy.
Penn State Hazleton & Schuylkill are continuing to deliver for students, families, and the entire region. Our entire region benefits from these two important local institutions, every day!

My bipartisan legislation to help address Pennsylvania’s long-term care workforce shortage was unanimously passed by the House of Representatives and signed by the Governor.
Senate Bill 116
will allow high school juniors and seniors to earn graduation credit by working or volunteering in licensed care settings that provide 24-hour care and supervision for the elderly.
Too many of our families, including mine, have faced the difficult decision of moving a parent or grandparent into a long-term care center. The professionals who provide their care are facing increasing challenges because of workforce shortages. This legislation will give students an opportunity to explore careers in long-term care while helping address this growing need.

The PA House unanimously passed, and the Governor signed
Senate Bill 381
, also known as the bipartisan “Beagle Bill.” I am a co-sponsor of this legislation. The “Beagle Bill” will prohibit the Commonwealth from funding animal testing and experiments. It will also protect dogs that were bred for testing and make animals previously in a lab available for adoption.
As you can see, our newest pup, Rufus, is growing up FAST! Every dog deserves a chance to live a happy, healthy life outside the lab. This bill is a major win for all those who love and care for animals.
